chapter: Looking back and the lean years
title: Steady jazz jobs have vanished, unlike Condon's tourist days
summary: He says clubs now change bands, whereas Condon's drew transients and charter buses for twelve and a half years; today maybe two steady bands exist in the US.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: That ended the house band idea - right?

Well, it certainly did and then they started to put in various kinds of music -- not that I have anything against that, but I always did well when I went there no matter what their policy was; even if they had far out guys or rock guys in there -- there were people that came to hear me that didn't come to hear the rock guys and, so, I did well there but I don't know how long I would have done well as a long period of time because I think bosses are right today to changing the policy--

At least changing bands - not having the same-- in the days of Condon when we went twelve and a half years on one job, I suppose everybody that ever came to New York came to Condon's. So, we weren't depending on the New Yorker; we were depending on the transients -- the people coming in from other countries.
You were a tourist attraction right?

Yes - right. We certainly were even to the point where they used to have chartered buses coming down there on special tours that people were paying for -- and this kind of thing but today -- well, just-- if you look around, just tell me one steady job for a jazz
Well, in the whole United States, I'd say maybe two where there's a band working steady all the time --
Yeah and those are bands that travel most the time - aren't they?

In that case I might say too that they're the local guys that got the job because, first of all, he can get it cheaper than bringing in a band from New York or bringing in a band from the West Coast and having to pay all the transportation and all that.
